paragraphs.heading: A loop of tropical air
paragraphs.text: The Walker circulation, also called the Walker cell, is a simplified picture of how air moves in the tropics within the lowest layer of the atmosphere, the troposphere. In this picture, bits of air travel round a closed loop, moving east or west and up or down. The model fits what is actually observed fairly well. The loop is driven by differences in how heat is spread between ocean and land. Tropical air also moves a great deal north and south, for example as part of the Hadley Circulation.

paragraphs.heading: Pressure and winds
paragraphs.text: Across the Pacific, the circulation goes along with a push from high air pressure over the eastern Pacific toward low air pressure over Indonesia. The tropical Indian, Pacific and Atlantic Oceans each have a Walker circulation. In northern summer they give westerly surface winds over the Indian Ocean but easterly winds over the Pacific and the Atlantic. That leaves the three oceans with very lopsided temperatures. The Pacific and Atlantic are cool at the surface in the east in northern summer, while the Indian Ocean is cooler only in the west.

paragraphs.heading: Wind and sea in a loop
paragraphs.text: The circulation changes over time together with changes in sea surface temperature. Some changes come from outside, such as the sun's seasonal shift into the Northern Hemisphere in summer. Others come from the ocean and air feeding each other, an idea first put forward by Bjerknes. Easterly winds cool the sea surface in the east, which sharpens the east–west heat contrast and strengthens the easterlies across the basin. The stronger easterlies bring more cold water up along the equator, cooling the east even more. From an ocean scientist's point of view, easterly winds are what cause the equatorial cold tongue.

paragraphs.heading: El Niño and La Niña
paragraphs.text: As first described, the Walker circulation is weaker during El Niño years. At those times both the temperature difference across the Pacific and the strength of the easterly winds are reduced. During La Niña years the reverse holds, and the circulation is stronger. Today the name may be used for a much wider spread of latitudes and longitudes, and may cover more than one region of overturning air.

paragraphs.heading: Named by Bjerknes
paragraphs.text: The name honours Gilbert Walker, who discovered the Southern Oscillation early in the twentieth century. The Norwegian-American meteorologist Jacob Bjerknes first used the term in 1969, for an east–west overturning loop he proposed near the Equator in the Pacific. He called its region of sinking air the arid zone. To the north and south of it lay the cloud bands of the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zones, which he saw as the equatorial edges of the Hadley Circulation in each hemisphere.

paragraphs.heading: Walker's work in India
paragraphs.text: In 1904 Walker, already an established applied mathematician at the University of Cambridge, took charge of India's observatories as director-general. There he studied the Indian Ocean monsoon, whose failed rains had caused severe famine in 1899. Working through huge amounts of weather data over the next fifteen years, he gave the first descriptions of a great seesaw in air pressure between the Indian and Pacific Oceans, and of how it tracked temperature and rainfall across much of the tropics. He rejected the earlier idea that sunspots drove temperature changes, showing that their monthly correlations were inconsistent. He also published every correlation he checked, useful or not, so other researchers would not chase links that were not real.
